displayed_attributes.title: Our experience and lessons learned from a security incident
displayed_attributes.body:
In March, we at [@Mintlify](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/company/25643) experienced a security incident that led to what I would describe to be one of the most challenging months in our company’s history.

Initially, I had no desire to share the experience. I wanted nothing more than to move on from the incident. However, while reflecting on the events and our mistakes, I realized that a lot of the lessons we learned the hard way might be helpful for other founders.

## What happened

On March 1, we discovered that within a timespan of 24 hours, attackers obtained several dozen of our customers’ private GitHub tokens. With these tokens, these attackers could gain read and write access our customer’s private repositories.

Needless to say, it was an “oh sh\*t” moment.

Upon discovering what had happened, we immediately revoked all GitHub tokens for everyone (not just those affected). It made the exposed tokens useless, but also disabled core parts of our product that relied on the tokens. Within the next three hour, we rotated our environment variables and implemented a number of emergency patches.

We knew that this was something we needed to inform our customers about, but decided against making the announcement immediately. We thought that publicizing the incident too quickly would attract more attacks before we were able to address the vulnerabilities employed in the incident, putting more customers at risk.

After unrooting the vulnerabilities and implementing a sweeping number of security measures, we posted the [incident report](https://mintlify.com/blog/incident-march-13) and notified all of our users on on March 13.

## The fallout

News began circulating through online forums regarding the incident. Some raised valid concerns. Others took it as an opportunity to criticize.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/434864/3e76dc7c-5809-468f-aac9-ad080e775346)

For the next few days, we would received a notifications every few minutes about someone posting something critical about us online.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/434864/c42d9c31-1fee-4bba-921b-317626c204e5)

We even made it to the top of HackerNews - a goal that I’ve aspired to for many years without success.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/434864/8c97fcd6-d24a-4b22-b560-39d84d39d49e)

Through all of the negative publicity, the most hurtful one for me was from a student who feared that our incident would have caused him to lose his internship.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/434864/d551be78-955a-48db-9abd-0339747a0b27)

Having been an intern in the not too distant past, the last thing I wanted was for someone to lose their job over our mistake.

I broke down. Throughout the whole incident, we chose not to respond and feed into the hate. But for that post, I just couldn’t resist. I wrote down everything that I could, hoping to equip them with everything that they needed to persuade their manager that it wasn’t their fault.

It turned out to be a mistake.

The next day, I got an email from Zack Whittaker from TechCrunch, who came across my response on that Reddit thread and pieced together a story from the information that was made available.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/434864/0af3c2e1-615c-4570-8cd1-51209d470c7a)

Within hours, the TechCrunch story came out.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/434864/ccc550cd-e312-4b30-a9d9-1468c5968b8f)

And in the following days, other tech news outlets picked it up as well.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/434864/47348a53-3570-4ea0-82fb-61b417dd85da)

The news had gotten out and it felt like everyone in the tech community had heard about the incident. My inbox became flooded with questions from reporters and customers.

After a week of non-stop bad PR, the news finally started to die down. I stopped getting notifications or messages about someone making a post or news article about the incident.

On March 22, we published our [security update](https://mintlify.com/blog/security-update) detailing everything that we’ve done to further fortify our product and ensure that an incident of similar nature or impact will never happen again.

After the security update was published, the whole security incident saga ended.

## Lessons learned

**Lesson 1. Increase security measures as you grow**

It’s common for founders to ignore security best-practices when they’re starting out in order to move fast. It’s hard to justify security when you don’t have any customer data to secure.

That’s what we did.

However, the mistake was not enabling better security best-practices as we grew. I fought to preserve the speed from our early days, and it came at the cost of security time and time again. That kind of thinking set us on the collision course for the incident to happen.

**Lesson 2. Checklist security is not the same as actual security**

We are SOC 2 certified and had penetration tests conducted every 6 months. However, the actual vulnerabilities that led to the incident were not uncovered by any of those tests or certifications.

The actual vulnerability that led to the incident was discovered and reported to us by a 17 year old on Twitter.

I am not suggesting that compliance and penetration tests aren’t useful - they very much are and certainly prevented us from many other attacks. But unfortunately in our case, solely jumping through these security hoops for enterprise procurement wasn’t enough. Truly having great security is an active effort that extends beyond the checklist and security theater.

**Lesson 3. Tough times build resilience**

A really memorable quote that got us through the endless stream of bad PR was a quote from Jensen Huang who said:

“…unfortunately, resilience matters in success. I don’t know how to teach it to you expect for I hope suffering happens to you”

Going through the incident was unbelievably difficult for the entire company, but it built in a tremendous amount of resilience. It made me more confident than every that we’ll be able to weather the storms of the future.

### Closing

I want to take an opportunity to thank the many founders in this community that supported us throughout the incident - particularly to [@Zeno Rocha](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/360041) and [@Vlad Matsiiako](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/942802).

top_comment.body:
Great writeup [@Han Wang](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/434864), and sorry to hear you went through such a difficult time.

This just goes to show how hard it is to get security right, especially when you have limited bandwidth and find yourself juggling many other priorities (that usually bring in money whereas security doesn't).

One piece of practical advice I can give is to work on eliminating security theater from your SOC 2 and security program. 

There have been few things I have seen that cause as much harm as the default one-size-fits-all cookiecutter SOC 2 programs that many platforms out there prescribe. These programs create a false sense of security, and infinitely worse, often lead companies to lean back assuming they're secure just to get hacked shortly after.

SOC 2 and security programs should be tailored to each individual company's needs and take into account the many specific risks and threats they face. Without this, even the best pentest in the world won't keep you safe.

Happy to help anyone explore if they're in a good place or not.

displayed_attributes.title: Launch Bookface: Thread (W23) - Incident Management for Large Enterprise
displayed_attributes.body:
Hi everyone! We’re Yuheng, Akeem, and Harsha, the co-founders of Thread. 

**tldr: Thread is incident management for large enterprises. We optimize the entire incident process by implementing targeted ticket routing, informed mitigation suggestions, and thorough post-incident analysis.**

### **Problem ❌:**

Incidents are the most stressful part of any live production service, and engineers are often ill-prepared for dealing with them… especially in large enterprises. As enterprises move to the cloud and microservice architecture, embrace remote work, and pick up increasingly more tooling for incidents, engineers face growing difficulty identifying and resolving complex system issues.

* APMs, such as Datadog and New Relic, **overwhelm engineers with data and lack contextual information, making problem-solving a challenge.**
* Customer support help desks, like Zendesk, **often provide inadequate information when creating tickets, leading to a frustrating cycle of questions for engineers.**
* Alerting and ITSM tools, such as Pagerduty and ServiceNow, **alert engineering teams but often lack the necessary context for efficient issue resolution.**

Not to mention, leadership still lacks visibility into incident details and progression.

It's like trying to solve a puzzle with missing pieces and no picture on the box.

### **Solution** 💡:

The gold standard for incident management workflows is straightforward to describe, but it is incredibly difficult to implement in practice, especially at enterprise scale.

The four pillars are:

**Detection**: identifying the bug using either a monitoring tool or a customer service tool

**Routing**: getting the ticket to the right person that can solve the issue, using paging tools and communication tools

**Resolution**: using context-providing tools like session replays and streamlined data providers to help solve the issue 

**Learning**: identifying the root cause of the issue and generating future workflows to more adeptly solve the problem (or prevent it from happening again) 

Enter **Thread:**

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/1146884/4379669d-6bb6-4f82-9cd4-97cdb2effe8f)

Thread offers engineers a customized configuration management database with runbooks, past tickets, monitoring data, and recommended actions for diagnosing and resolving incidents.

We also provide real-time updates and summaries to leadership and stakeholders during critical incidents, identifying bottlenecks in workflows to prevent future issues.

Why settle for a single tool that might not fit all your needs? Our platform allows teams to bring in their favorite tools to create a tailor-made solution.

![uploaded image](/media/?key=user_uploads/1146884/cfa81e00-5c44-45dc-b648-ecfeec726a3b)

### **Why us?**

We’re 3 ex-Microsoft/Amazon engineers who built these tools and processes on our respective teams (Microsoft Store and Prime Video). We want to take what we learned and build an even better solution for the millions of engineers out there, so no one has to face the existential dread of on-call panic ever again. 

### **Our Ask** ❤️:

If you or anyone in your network knows a VP/Director of Engineering at a large enterprise, around fortune 5000 level, (**bonus points if their org currently uses tools like ServiceNow**) who would be open to using a 3rd party tool to improve their incident management, processes, and/or learnings, **we’d love an intro.**

If you have enterprise-level experience with **any of the above tools, we want to hear from you!** We're always striving to improve our integrations and bridge any gaps in the incident management process. Share your experiences with us!

Reach out to us at [**founders@usethread.io**](mailto:founders@usethread.io)! We’d love to chat!

displayed_attributes.title: Launch BF: IncidentFox (W26) | Turning “we have no logs for this” into an impossibility
displayed_attributes.body:
# ****

Every startup I talk to has the same story: production breaks, they go to check logs, and… nothing useful. We’ve been
building an AI SRE agent and learned a painful lesson: you can’t debug incidents when there’s nothing to debug with.
Most startups have garbage observability because nobody has time to add proper logging, metrics, and tracing. It’s
boring work that only matters when things break.

**New approach: auto-instrument at PR time**

We’re building a code review agent that scans your org’s repos and automatically adds:

  - Structured logging at key code paths
  - Metrics for the things you’ll actually need to debug
  - Distributed tracing spans
  - Consistent conventions across all services

It runs on every PR. Engineers write features, we handle the telemetry. No more “can you add logging for this?” comments
that get ignored.

**Why this unlocks everything else**

Since we’re adding all the instrumentation, we know your entire system:

  - Auto-generated service maps and dependency graphs
  - Pre-built dashboards without any manual setup
  - Intelligent alerting based on actual code paths
  - When incidents DO happen, our AI SRE has full context of the codebase and telemetry

**The pitch:** Reliability-as-a-service that starts at code review, not at 3am pages.

**Who wants to never write another logging line?**

We’re looking for 3-5 startups to design partner with. You’d get:

  - Free auto-instrumentation on your repos
  - Auto-generated dashboards
  - Early access to the AI SRE with full codebase context

DM me or comment below.

displayed_attributes.title: Benchmark your Incident Management Practices against other YC companies!
displayed_attributes.body:
**Have you wondered whether you're following the best practices for incident management?**

We are conducting a study on **Best Practices for Incident Management**  by interviewing 20+ CTOs/engineering managers/engineers and sharing consolidated results with the participants so you can benchmark yourself. If you are interested, email me at gaurav@rootly.io or leave a comment below. 

**Am I the right person for it?** 
Yes, if - 
- A production issue(incident) can impact your customer's ability to use your product resulting in lost revenue(e.g. e-Commerce) or churned customers(e.g. Twilio). 
- Your team deals with >1 incident/week.
- Your engineering team > 10 engineers and have an on-call rotation (resulting in a need for co-ordination). 

**What will I learn?**
- What are the biggest pain points engineering teams face with incident management? 
- How are they getting better at managing incidents as a team? 
- What are the key metrics they are tracking related to incidents? 
- What tools/best practices/culture have they put in place to better manage and reduce incidents? 
- Postmortem best practices


Feel free to comment below or email me directly (gaurav@rootly.io)
If there is a question you'd love to know the answer to, let me know and I'll add it to my list.

Measure What Matters!   
-Gaurav    
P.S. We already have this data from 3 companies (including 2 YC unicorns) that have had to scale up their services pretty fast in the past few years. Will be sharing some interesting learnings from them as well!
